title: Teen who singer D4vd is accused of killing had multiple abortions, texts reveal
description: WARNING: Readers may find details in this article distressing.Texts between singer D4vd and Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old he is accused of
body: WARNING: Readers may find details in this article distressing.Texts between singer D4vd and Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old he is accused of murdering, reveal she had been pregnant and had had an abortion before her death. The messages were shown during a hearing for a judge to determine if the singer, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, should go on trial for the teen's death last year."What [if] the first abortion didn't work?" Celeste texted Burke in June 2024, according to prosecutors. She was 13 years old at the time and he was 19. Prosecutors say Burke killed her after she threatened to reveal he had been abusing a minor and destroy his career. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing the girl.In an exchange from January 2024, Burke apologised to the teen for "putting her through this", according to messages shown in the Los Angeles court on Friday.She responded, "neither of us are capable of watching and taking care of the baby. it's for the best no?"Burke asked, "also my mother always told me to ask this question if I was ever in this situation … it is mine right?" Celeste replied "of course its yours David", according to testimony from a detective.The court heard that in another text to the teen, sent in June 2024, Burke wrote: "Let's let this abortion be the last one til we have the real one…" Prosecutors presented iCloud data recovered from the defendant's iPhone, showing texts between him and Celeste dating back to 8 August 2022, when she was 11 years old and he was 17.The device belonging to Burke also had photos of the teenager during the alleged sexual abuse, prosecutors and Los Angeles Police Detective Corey Farell said on Friday.The victim's mother, Mercedes Rivas Hernandez, became visibly emotional and left the court with her husband as details of some of the pictures were described during the proceedings. Burke's phone also showed conversations the two had had about moving in together, which they had dubbed "Operation Awesome".The pair "broke up" in November 2024, but stayed in contact, according to a memo filed by prosecutors earlier this year. Prosecutors allege they argued on the night before her death, allegedly over Burke's relationships with other women.Dr Grant Ho of the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner, who conducted the post-mortem examination on Celeste, also testified on Friday.Ho told the court it was "extremely difficult to tell" exactly when the girl died, owing to the state of decomposition when her remains were found.Lawyers for the defence seized on that uncertainty, questioning whether it was possible that the teenager could have somehow harmed herself. Farrell, the police detective, testified that DNA taken from blood found in Burke's Hollywood Hills home and garage was a match for Celeste.D4vd, who rose to fame on TikTok with the viral hits Romantic Homicide and Here With Me, was on tour when police found Celeste's body in the front boot of his Tesla in September 2025 - the day after she would have turned 15. His worldwide tour was cancelled and he largely retreated from public life and social media.Police announced his arrest in April this year.Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman has filed seven criminal charges against him, including murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child and the mutilation of remains.They said the teen was reported missing by her family and was last seen at Burke's home on 3 April 2025 - five months before her remains were discovered in the Tesla.Prosecutors have said he met Celeste online when she was 11, and allege he started sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18. Friday marked the fourth day of testimony in the pre-trial hearing. Earlier revelations by prosecutors included that Hernandez had been brought by Burke to London and Texas to meet members of his family there. Testimony is expected to resume on Monday.

schema.headline: Teen who singer D4vd is accused of killing had multiple abortions, texts reveal

title: Trump orders Smithsonian to post warnings about 'inaccurate' US history
description: President Donald Trump has ordered signs to be placed outside the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, to caution visitors about exhibits
body: President Donald Trump has ordered signs to be placed outside the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, to caution visitors about exhibits his administration views as "inaccurate".The order directs the Department of Interior to issue the warnings, and also to direct people about where they can find "accurate information regarding America's history".The Trump administration has often accused the Smithsonian Institution, the world's largest research museum, as well as other academic organisations of harbouring an anti-American bias.The Smithsonian did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment. The order on Friday - titled Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution - accuses museum leadership of not doing enough to celebrate America's founders on the country's 250th anniversary of independence, which took place on 4 July.It says the museum's leadership team "views American history as a 'prime tool' to advance ideas of social justice and the radical transformation of our society".An accompanying White House statement, external also accused the museum of  veering "toward extreme political activism, rooted in Marxism, to divide, dispirit, and discourage Americans".Democrats who oversee the Smithsonian condemned the order."This EO is a clear political overreach, driven by an ideological agenda to rewrite American history," congresswoman Melanie Stansbury, ranking member of the House Administration Committee, wrote on X. "Our Smithsonian institutions do not belong to the President, but to the American people and so does our nation's history."The executive order comes just days after Smithsonian director Anthea Hartig was grilled by Republican lawmakers in two congressional hearings, where the museum was accused of being "infected by a woke ideology that seeped into public displays, educational materials and planning documents".Earlier this month, the White House Domestic Policy Council released a scathing report, claiming that the museum "erases our heritage".Trump has set out to radically reshape American culture, which he says has been contaminated by "woke" left-wing ideology. He has signed several orders that are intended to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion programmes from the federal government - some of which led to legal challenges.In March, he issued a separate order against the Smithsonian, directing it to "eliminate improper, divisive, or anti-American ideology".The Smithsonian is largely funded by the federal government. Its museums offer free entry to some 15 to 30 million visitors each year. It operates 21 museums in Washington, Virginia and New York.They include the National Museum of American History, the National Portrait Gallery, the American Art Museum, the National Zoo and more than a dozen others.

schema.headline: Trump orders Smithsonian to post warnings about 'inaccurate' US history

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Gabriel Langton injury overshadows gymnastics silver
description: A sickening injury to England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in G
body: A sickening injury to England's Gabriel Langton overshadowed his team's silver medal in the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.The 19-year-old, from the City of Birmingham Gymnastics Club, needed lengthy treatment on the mat after a horrible fall in the final rotation of the evening at The Arena.Langton fell head first to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar, three metres in the air, leading to a lengthy delay to the action as he was tended to by up to a dozen medical staff.He was eventually led away on a trolley after being moved on to a stretcher with his head and neck braced and left to huge applause from the packed crowd who had spent much of the previous 10 minutes in hushed silence.Langton was seen to be conscious and moving his legs and arms before leaving the arena floor, while team officials later said he was moving and speaking to doctors.In a statement, Team England said: "We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance."He has been taken to hospital and we will share more information when it is available."When competition resumed, his England team-mates were unable to overhaul their deficit to Canada who claimed their first gold medal in the event in 20 years, having finished second to England at the past two games.Langton, a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock,  was unable to join his teammates on the podium as England collected their silver medals.Team-mate Luke Whitehouse, who was first on to the apparatus after the competition restarted and posted a relatively low score of 11.700, said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time." Whitehouse added: "From what we've heard, he's doing OK. Gymnastics is such a dangerous sport and things like this remind us of that. It's one of those things you have to put out of your mind."Felix Dolci, who helped Canada to gold and led qualifying for the all-around competition, said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes. "All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. Pushing through this is definitely not easy, England stayed focussed, they stayed in the zone, a huge shout out to them because that's not an easy one. "For any gymnast that was on the field of play, seeing this not only is difficult, but something you never want to see. It goes to show how hard the sport is."Hamish Carter from Team Scotland - who narrowly missed out on a bronze medal to Australia in the final rotation - said: "I didn't actually see what happened. I'm just so happy that he's alright and, having experienced that, anything could have happened. "We've walked away with no medal but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment."

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Gabriel Langton injury overshadows gymnastics silver

title: Schedule changes called for after Jannik Sinner and Novak Djokovic withdraw from Canadian Open
description: The tournament director of the Canadian Open says changes need to be made to the "demanding schedule" of players after Jannik Sinner and Novak Djokovi
body: The tournament director of the Canadian Open says changes need to be made to the "demanding schedule" of players after Jannik Sinner and Novak Djokovic pulled out of the Masters 1000 event.Sinner, who beat Alexander Zverev to win the Wimbledon title this month, said he had withdrawn from the ATP tournament, which takes place from 2-13 August in Montreal, to prioritise his health.Carlos Alcaraz will also be absent from the Canadian Open as he continues his recovery from a wrist injury that has kept him out since April."We are obviously very disappointed that Jannik and Novak won't be joining us in Montreal this year, especially after they also withdrew from last year's tournament in Toronto," said the Canadian Open's tournament director Valerie Tetreault."We respect their decisions and understand that, with such a demanding schedule, players' health must remain the priority."That said, we believe the frequency of these last-minute withdrawals in the last few years raises a broader issue for our sport. "Masters 1000 events are among the flagship tournaments on the tour, and fans rightfully expect to see the world's best compete."We are already in discussions with the ATP to ensure this matter received serious consideration."The Canadian Open takes place before the Cincinnati Open, which is also a Masters 1000 event, and prior to the start of the US Open - the final Grand Slam of the year - on 30 August.Seven of the existing nine Masters 1000 events - the sport's highest level below the Grand Slams - are now staged over 12 days and concerns over the congested tennis calendar, which stretches across 11 months of the year for the top players, have regularly been voiced.Britain's Jack Draper and Emma Raducanu recently pulled out of Wimbledon on the eve of their home Grand Slam because of injury.Draper, who withdrew with a long-term arm injury, said he felt the amount of injuries suffered by leading players is "pretty worrying".In September 2024, Alcaraz said: "They are going to kill us in some way.""We firmly believe adjustments are needed in the near future to better protect the integrity of our Masters 1000 events while remaining mindful of the realities players face," added Tetreault.Earlier this year, women's world number one Aryna Sabalenka and Iga Swiatek pulled out of the Dubai Championships, a WTA 1000 event, two days before it started.Tournament director Salah Tahlak said players who made late withdrawals from tournaments should be docked points, while Sabalenka said criticism of her was "ridiculous" and that she may not play at the tournament again.

schema.headline: Schedule changes called for after Jannik Sinner and Novak Djokovic withdraw from Canadian Open

title: Noah Lyles wins 100m at US championships in world-leading 9.79s
description: Noah Lyles ran a world-leading 9.79 seconds as he claimed an impressive victory in the 100m at the US athletics championships.He also equalled his per
body: Noah Lyles ran a world-leading 9.79 seconds as he claimed an impressive victory in the 100m at the US athletics championships.He also equalled his personal best, which he set in winning gold at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, with the run at the Icahn Stadium in New York City.The previous best 100m in 2026 was the 9.82 set by Jamaica's Oblique Seville in June."I think I made that 'I'm still the world's fastest man' statement," said Lyles.The 29-year-old American finished ahead of Ronnie Baker in second and third-placed Kenny Bednarek, who were both given a time of 9.88, while former world champion Christian Coleman was fourth in 9.93."Just because it is an off year doesn't mean that I plan to run slow," added Lyles, referring to there being no Olympics or World Championships this year. "This is me being me and being me is dominant, being consistent."Sha'Carri Richardson, the 2023 world champion, won the women's 100m as she clocked 10.77.The 26-year-old equalled her best time of the season as Kayla White finished second with 10.90 and Tamari Davis third in 11.00."It just feels phenomenal to be back in a better place, just healthy mentally, physically and emotionally," said Richardson, who has had troubles off the track."Everything me and coach have been working on, it's starting to show consistently."

schema.headline: Noah Lyles wins 100m at US championships in world-leading 9.79s

title: Graduation outfits: Students tell us how to impress on a budget
description: "My mum is a designer so she made this for me," says Wendy. "It took her a week… I'm her daughter, so she had to put in every [effort]."Wendy says the
body: "My mum is a designer so she made this for me," says Wendy. "It took her a week… I'm her daughter, so she had to put in every [effort]."Wendy says the significance of graduation inspired her to create a custom look. "I feel like you have to because it's your day. We go through a lot to get a master's degree so you have to look your best on the day."Graduation also comes at a time when students are "the least financially resilient", says Allingham, as they have been absorbing the costs of studying all year.The maintenance loan falls short of living costs by an average of £502 per month, according to analysis by Save The Student, external. This gap is plugged - sometimes only partially - by parental support, part-time jobs and debt.Another factor that can increase the cost of graduation is buying an official photograph, with providers specified by your university, adds Allingham. "The price of photography on the day - it's extortionate."Professional packages at the University of Salford start at £30 - an image of the graduate is sent digitally - and the most expensive is £350. For that you receive about 20 prints with various mounts and frames of two images, one of the graduate and another with friends and family.Like Keerthana, Alicia Munhupedzi used the internet to find her dress - though it was a bit last minute."I thought, 'Where can I get a nice dress really quickly and cheaply?'" The answer? Depop, the second-hand clothing app popular among Gen Z shoppers that sold for $1.2bn (£890m) earlier this year.Like others, Alicia felt her outfit was important. "Graduation, it's a milestone thing, especially if you're not planning on doing a master's," she says. "So, to me, there was a pressure."So much so she couldn't sleep properly the night before her ceremony and woke at dawn to get ready. "I made it through today off two hours of sleep, water, good vibes, energy and a coffee."Knowing all eyes would be fixed on her when she was handed her degree, Keerthana says she was nervous for her graduation ceremony - but it passed more quickly than she thought it might."This is the only moment you get for yourself," she says. And was the 05:00 wake-up and two hours of getting ready worth it? "Yeah," Keerthana says, "I couldn't compromise on that."Additional reporting by Kate Berry and George Sandeman.

schema.headline: Graduation outfits: Students tell us how to impress on a budget

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Summer of chaos' and 'water bosses' pay rises'
description: Pictures of tourists on a beach in France, with a huge cloud of black smoke from wildfires burning in the distance, are on several front pages. "Europ
body: Pictures of tourists on a beach in France, with a huge cloud of black smoke from wildfires burning in the distance, are on several front pages. "Europe ablaze" says the FT Weekend, external. "Summer of chaos" is the Daily Mirror's headline, external. It says thousands of British holidaymakers are facing huge queues to travel to mainland Europe, while fires rage.The Times says, external it's seen a report which says the UK is at a greater risk of blackouts because of the drive towards renewable energy. The paper says in the era of fossil fuel power plants, the national grid operator could easily monitor its output and balance demand and supply, minute by minute - but that's become much more difficult with the emergence of wind farms, solar panels and batteries. One whistleblower claims the grid operator is now "flying blind."On its front page the Daily Telegraph says, external Iran is sending its operatives to the UK in migrant boats. The paper says Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps controls some of the people smuggling routes across Europe. An unnamed Iranian official says the regime could easily make London unsafe if it wanted to. The Home Office has been approached for comment.According to FT Weekend, external, the new Chancellor, John Healey, is under mounting pressure to raise taxes or find savings, because the government's fiscal buffer has been eroded to a "razor thin level". The paper says renewed fighting in the Middle East has increased the cost of government borrowing, while Andy Burnham has made new spending commitments with measures to support households and small businesses.An investigation by the Daily Mail, external has found that some parents are being financially crippled, or driven to suicide, because of "massively inflated" child maintenance charges. The paper says "appalling blunders" by the Child Maintenance Service have led to people being overcharged several thousand pounds a month; some have lost their homes and at least two fathers have taken their own lives. The agency denies having significant issues with its IT system.And the Sun says, external Madonna is in talks to play a record three consecutive nights at BST Hyde Park in London next summer. If she does, the paper says, around 210,000 people are expected to attend, but sources close to her say nothing has been decided.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Summer of chaos' and 'water bosses' pay rises'

title: Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids
description: Image source, Nilly DahliaImage caption, Nilly Dahlia says she wants her kids to enjoy a "nostalgic summer"ByEmily HoltThe six-week summer holidays ha
body: Image source, Nilly DahliaImage caption, Nilly Dahlia says she wants her kids to enjoy a "nostalgic summer"ByEmily HoltThe six-week summer holidays have officially begun and, for many parents, finding exciting but affordable activities for children can be tough. For most families in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the break is already under way. In Scotland, children have enjoyed some time off already, but will return to school earlier than those elsewhere in the UK.Here are five tips to help children get the most out of the next few weeks of summer. 1. Not every holiday has to be abroad A family's first instinct when summer is approaching may be to look at booking a trip abroad, but rising costs and travel expenses mean a holiday isn't feasible for everyone. Mags Rivett, director at Family Holiday Charity, which supports families with UK trips, says there are many benefits to arranging time away with children that don't require expensive travel. She says the social aspect of a holiday can help children develop their communication skills. "Lots of kids have never really had the opportunity to meet people outside of their own community," Rivett says. "But if you go somewhere that's got social facilities, it's a really important opportunity."She says getting recommendations from friends and family is a good place to start. Rivett gives the example of Skegness, a coastal holiday destination in Lincolnshire, accessible by train or coach, which her charity has supported families to visit.A family-of-four's accommodation in a holiday park there this August starts at around £750 for a week, while an off-peak return train from Manchester would cost around £280 for four.By contrast, a last-minute trip to Majorca for a family-of-four at that time starts from around £2,000. Better deals can usually be found booking further in advance.2. Prioritise the moments, not the cost Samantha Thomas, creator of Budget Mum UK, says she focuses on the time she can give her children, rather than the money she could spend on a day out. Thomas suggests focusing on your budget first to understand what you can comfortably spend, and then build your activities around that, to help remove any "stress or guilt" during the holidays. "Children don't need a six-week programme of expensive activities," Thomas says. "Some of the memories that they'll treasure most will come from simple things, like baking together or a picnic in the park, or building a den in the living room."Ingredients to bake fairy cakes with buttercream icing usually cost between £10 and £15 - depending on what you already have in the cupboard.For a picnic - or picky bits - prices can vary. But it can easily be done on a budget of around £5. Image source, Samantha ThomasImage caption, Samantha Thomas says treasured family memories can be created on a budgetTasneem Abdur-Rashid, an author and single mum of two, echoes Thomas' opinion and wants to relieve the pressure she puts on herself to do something different with her children every day. She says it's important to take time out, put work away, and spend one-on-one time with your children. This could be going to play in the park, or going swimming.Trips to local pools or lidos can cost around £6 for adults, and £3.50 for children.Abdur-Rashid says every night during the holidays she will play board games with her children, which blends quality time and fun. These can be picked up at local charity shops for very reasonable prices."You don't even have to leave the house for that," she says, "and they love it."3. Use what's available in your area Nilly Dahlia, a content creator and mum of three, says she prints out a six-week calendar with a range of activities for her kids during the holidays. As part of their "summer bucket list", they are planning to check out all the parks in the local area and she is prioritising low-cost activities throughout the summer. "I feel like there's this intense pressure to have Instagram-worthy holidays now," she says."What's wrong with just staying in the UK, staying out till sunset, riding your bike, just going to the river, like I did? I really want the kids to experience a nostalgic summer."Dahlia stresses there are many things on offer during the holidays that won't break the bank, such as free kids' meals in cafes and discounts on local travel. And there are often offers at bowling venues and cinemas, she says, while her family enjoys a movie night at home every Friday."They each have a bowl of popcorn and treats and we move the sofas into two rows so it's like a cinema."James Gray, communications and advocacy manager at Libraries Connected, says the summer holidays are also where libraries "come alive". He says libraries across the UK will hold the Summer Reading Challenge, encouraging kids to read more in a fun format, and many will be hosting events such as arts and crafts, performances and creative workshops, all for free. 4. Balance rest with some learningDahlia says she picks up books for her children to get them ready for the next school year. Her youngest will receive some chapter books to help them transition into Year 3, while her eldest is moving to secondary school, and Dahlia has prepped suitable books to bridge that gap from primary.She preps "summer baskets" which include puzzle books, reading books and snacks  to curb any boredom. "It's so important because by reading, they're still engaging their brain so they can go back to school in September, already having vocabulary in them."As a busy parent, Abdur-Rashid says she doesn't always have the time to do everything she'd like with her children, but structures their days to make sure they are always doing an activity. She allocates an hour a day for gaming which her boys enjoy, and then fills the rest of the time with playing, reading or writing. She also wants to foster a passion for reading in her kids, and allows them to not finish books they don't enjoy so reading doesn't become a "punishment".Image source, Tasneem Abdur-RashidImage caption, Author Tasneem Abdur-Rashid suggests parks and picnics for low-cost quality time with your childrenGavin Morgan, an education psychologist at University College London, says it's important to let children be "bored" during the holidays. "It's really important that they have opportunities to switch off from school and from that structure in order to experience and explore new things and get bored, because for some kids, that can really spark that creativity."For those entering exam years, Morgan says parents should have a conversation with their child about what they need to do and what suits them best. "The worst thing for parents to do is put their child under any kind of pressure, because they'll end up being switched off from learning," he says.He says parents should encourage their children to take a break from their education, so they return to school in September "feeling really confident and refreshed".5. Get ahead for the next holidays Thomas says she starts planning her summer budget well in advance. She does this by contributing a little bit of money every month into a "sinking fund" - a pot of money set aside for a specific purpose.This summer her budget is £500, and she sits down with her children to discuss how much they have budgeted and to brainstorm activities they can do together. "You've got that open dialogue, so they understand there's only a finite amount of money, and we've got a plan on how to do that best," she says.Thomas also uses cashback websites to get money back on things she has bought, which she says is "brilliant for hotels or travel". If you are planning a holiday, whether abroad or in the UK, Thomas stresses to plan and book in advance to get better deals. She also recommends looking at attractions within your local area before travelling further afield. Additional reporting by Hayley Clarke

schema.headline: Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids

title: Commonwealth Games: Adam Ramsay-Peaty ready for 'scrap' with apprentice Filip Nowacki
description: Adam Ramsay-Peaty becomes the latest to face the latter situation on Saturday - in the 100m breaststroke final at Glasgow's Commonwealth Games, shortl
body: Adam Ramsay-Peaty becomes the latest to face the latter situation on Saturday - in the 100m breaststroke final at Glasgow's Commonwealth Games, shortly after 21:00 BST.The greatest breaststroker the world has seen is on his own journey - one which he hopes ends with a third individual gold at the Los Angeles Olympics in two years' time.Manoeuvring into his slipstream is 18-year-old Filip Nowacki.Master meet apprentice.Not only has Nowacki started to pick off Ramsay-Peaty's age-group records, he is part of the 31-year-old's AP Race stable - the programme set up to develop the next generation.Ramsay-Peaty has spoken of wanting to mentor and pass on advice to his young pretender. Last year, Nowacki repaid him by breaking his 100m breaststroke junior British record.Ramsay-Peaty, who is chasing a 33rd major gold of a glittering career, appeared in no mood to hand over the baton in Friday's semi-finals.There is uncertainty around a broken finger suffered in June but, side by side in lanes four and five, Ramsay-Peaty built an early lead and held off the youngster in the second length. Nowacki was close but never quite close enough."I saw his front wave, but at the same time that is what I train for," Ramsay-Peaty said."I know I am a sprinter. I know I can go out fast."Nowacki, who competes for Jersey here having learned to swim under the tutelage of Nathan Jegou on the Channel Island, is arguably best in the 200m event - a distance Ramsay-Peaty does not race.In this shorter contest, it is the youngster who should stay stronger for longer.And when they spoke afterwards alongside each other, Ramsay-Peaty, all chest and tattooed muscle, towered over his young rival - so much so you would be forgiven for thinking the pair compete in different sports.Nowacki appeared wary of Ramsay-Peaty but there is a cheeky confidence within."Course I do," he laughed when asked if he believes he can win."No, I wish, I'm gonna give it my best shot" was his quick addition.Nowacki was not long out of armbands when Ramsay-Peaty won gold in this same pool at the 2014 Commonwealth Games.That was his emergence on to the global stage and two years later the Englishman won his first Olympic title in Rio de Janeiro. Nowacki was only eight years old."Adam is a true role model in the sport," Nowacki said."I grew up watching him race at Rio, Tokyo and Paris."To race him and not be a random competitor but give him a race is special to me."The pair should compete as Team GB team-mates in LA but are also racing for their own personal ambitions on Saturday.Despite winning an emotional silver at the Olympics in Paris two years ago, Ramsay-Peaty has not stood atop a major podium since the Birmingham Commonwealth Games in 2022.In that meet he won the 50m crown but lost his 100m title to James Wilby. A "self-destructive spiral" amid issues with his mental health, which led to him considering his future in the sport, soon followed.If Nowacki wins a medal it would be Jersey's first at the Commonwealth Games for 36 years. They have only ever won one gold medal.Australia's Sam Williamson, who won the first semi-final, will also have something to say."It is going to be a good scrap, especially down that last 25m, and I do love a good scrap," Ramsay-Peaty said.He would never go quietly.

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games: Adam Ramsay-Peaty ready for 'scrap' with apprentice Filip Nowacki

title: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes
description: Image source, KJA Photography/Kimberley AppletonImage caption, Courtney and Sam Scholey had their dream wedding day at a venue in the Oxfordshire coun
body: Image source, KJA Photography/Kimberley AppletonImage caption, Courtney and Sam Scholey had their dream wedding day at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside - only it wasn't legalByTiffanie TurnbullThe day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham."For us, that day was as insignificant as possible,"  Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses. "I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Wedding rules date back to the 18th and 19th CenturiesCurrently, a marriage or civil partnership ceremony in England or Wales must take place at an approved venue to be legally binding – and many exert control on elements of the wedding such as vows, headcounts or music.There are also tight restrictions on who can officiate a wedding and how. Authorised religious figures can, but – with few exceptions – only in places of worship. Registrars can conduct a wedding, but it can't have any religious content. And celebrants can't legally marry people at all.A Law Commission report in 2022 concluded that these marriage laws, which date back to the 18th and 19th Centuries, were "complicated, inefficient, unfair and needlessly restrictive".David Lammy, then deputy prime minister, said marriage laws in England and Wales had "not kept pace with the social and cultural changes that have shaped modern Britain".He added: "Some feel forced to pay for two different ceremonies, one legal and one belief based. Some enter into a marriage that isn't legally recognised. Others feel they have little choice but to marry in a way which doesn't reflect their beliefs, marring what should be a joyous occasion."Scotland and Northern Ireland relaxed their rules years ago. Though the exact shape of the new rules is still under public consultation until September, these changes will take regulations from a "buildings based" regulation model to an "officiant based" one.'The laws are now, what, 200 years out of date?'Brown said she and her partner had put off getting married because there was no legal and affordable version of a wedding that reflects them.She said she didn't want bells and whistles - or even a wedding dress. "I just want somebody to marry us and in a beautiful setting that isn't just going to cost the earth."Brown went on to explain that she'd been scared her mum - who is 86 and unwell - would miss out on her wedding day. But these proposals had given her hope: "The laws are now, what, 200 years out of date?"Miranda Allard, 66, agreed that change is long overdue.When she got married 40 years ago, she had to jump through hoops to get permission to hold an interfaith ceremony in her parent's garden - and finds it astounding couples today face the same obstacles."We applied for a special licence... [and] explained how we did not want to put my Jewish mother-in-law through a church wedding," she said."I, on the other hand, was brought up in a Christian family and would not 'feel married' if doing so in a registry office."It took letters from the couple, their parents, the local bishop, the village vicar and more to convince authorities to allow the ceremony."We also combined our legal Christian service with Jewish prayers and tradition, like breaking the glass. Totally unheard of then and ever since," she said, adding the nuptials even made the paper.Image source, Miranda AllardImage caption, Simon and Miranda Allard had to get permission to hold an interfaith ceremony in her parent's garden when they got married 40 years ago... Image source, Miranda AllardImage caption, ... their nuptials even made the paper Father John, who didn't provide his last name, wrote in to BBC Your Voice to say he'd like to be able to perform ceremonies like this too."Marriage is about the lifelong commitment made before God for me, and for some couples the setting can make that sacred moment even more personal and memorable."Brian Bracher, 65, from Chichester in West Sussex, said he cannot believe the UK is still debating these changes."It is ridiculous that, in this modern era, a small minority are still trying to exert control and make decisions about what is frivolous and not acceptable. Just let people, that love each other, marry in a way that suits them."The proposals will be a welcome change for Christians from the LGBT community, said 33-year-old Isabel Sinagola. She added: "[They] currently cannot have the wedding they might want, as they cannot marry in the Church of England, but also cannot have religious content in the only option available to them: a civil ceremony." Others are hopeful this provides more affordable wedding options.'We want to get married but won't, as it costs too much'Carl Jones said he and his partner of 20 years haven't wed because even the simplest weddings are too expensive."We want to get married but won't, as it costs too much. It's cheaper if we just have two witnesses, but why should our [12-year-old] daughter not be allowed to attend... It's wrong."But sceptics say this will do little to lower the cost of weddings, which according to wedding planner app Hitched has jumped to £21,990 on average.Reverend Tom Kennar said it isn't marriage that is expensive, it's the extras most modern couples like to add."[It] is the costs of the reception, vehicles, booze, photographers, clothing, food, cars etc," he said.Other critics of the proposal say they fear it will dilute the significance of marriage."Marriage is a gift from God to secure society. Not an opportunity to set new standards and styles," said Donald Tosh, from Glasgow, who wrote to BBC Your Voice."It's now not a life decision, it's a temporary decision. And now with this, a very temporary frivolous decision," said Oliver, from Kent.However, celebrant Zadie Ward told the BBC the changes could enhance the meaning of a wedding for many couples."[Critics] are saying it's a solemn promise and it's about the serious commitment, but how can you ask someone to make a serious commitment in words that mean nothing to them and ways that are meaningless to them?"Image source, Sophie Ann PhotographyImage caption, "Modern relationships deserve modern ceremonies," says celebrant Zadie Ward She says the changes won't take anything from those who still want traditional weddings – it simply gives couples who don't more options."You've got blended families, mixed cultures, traditions that are changing even within those cultures. "Modern relationships deserve modern ceremonies."The government has stressed there will be safeguards to guarantee the dignity of marriage is preserved.Ceremonies deemed to be "gimmicks" that risk trivialising the legal act of marriage would not be allowed. Activities "such as skydiving, white-water rafting, roller coasters or other amusement rides" would "fall short of the standard"."Every couple deserves to start their journey together with an unforgettable day that reflects their beliefs, their personalities and the lives they plan to build together," Lammy wrote."This Government's changes will bring weddings law into the twenty-first century."Additional reporting by Mary Litchfield and Rozina Sini

schema.headline: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes

title: Who could be the next Graham Norton, and does the BBC even need one?
description: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?Image caption, Winkleman steppd down from her chat show last w
body: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?Image caption, Winkleman steppd down from her chat show last week following its seven-episode runBySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporterWhen Lisa Kudrow appeared on The Claudia Winkleman Show earlier this year, she was visibly delighted to meet Linda from The Traitors. The Friends actress, probably the most famous guest the programme had during its seven-week run, said it was "thrilling" to meet one of the reality show's breakout stars, who she revealed had even inspired one of her own recent performances.As host of The Traitors, Winkleman was ideally placed to introduce the pair, resulting in the kind of wonderfully bizarre meeting of minds normally seen on The Graham Norton Show. But Winkleman's own chat show did not last long enough for any more unusual guest combinations on its teal sofa. The presenter quit last week after just one series, saying she was simply "too nervous to enjoy it". It had made sense for the BBC to commission The Claudia Winkleman Show, given the presenter's popularity on programmes such as Strictly.There's a different level of pressure, however, hosting a show with your own name above the door. Image caption, Lisa Kudrow (second left) said she was "thrilled" to meet Linda from the Traitors (far right) on the chat show"Everyone thought she could pull it off because she's smart and funny, but a chat show with multiple guests is very difficult to handle," the Telegraph's arts and entertainment editor, Anita Singh, tells BBC News."You have to marshall the conversation, give each guest equal time, help them to plug whatever they're plugging, then cue in whatever anecdote they've agreed beforehand with the researchers. Graham Norton makes that look deceptively easy."She adds: "I think if Claudia had done a couple more series she would have become better at it. But she's at her best when she's being spontaneous, and the format allows very little space for that."Winkleman's decision to quit surprised many. The viewing figures were lower than Norton's, but still respectable. The reviews from critics were mixed, rather than universally bad. The BBC confirmed it was Winkleman's decision to stop, and implied that they would've happily commissioned a second series - and possibly already had. "My understanding is they had made a deal beyond one season," says Deadline's Jake Kanter, who has reported on the talk show throughout. "How formal that was, I don't know. But there was an intention for it to continue."He adds: "I wholeheartedly believe her that this perhaps didn't work out because of her own concerns and anxiety around the hosting."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Winkleman's chat show was made by Graham Norton's production company So TelevisionFormer BBC One controller Peter Fincham, who hosts the TV podcast Insiders, likens it to the Davina McCall chat show he commissioned in 2006, which also ended after one series. "You have to remember, particularly chat shows where the presenter's name is in the title, it's very exposing for them," he tells BBC News. "Had Claudia Winkleman wanted to carry on with her chat show, it could have been a slow burn," he reflects. "But what she's done is rare, actually, for somebody to say, 'hmm, didn't really enjoy that, don't think I'll do it again'. "That says something very positive about her that you don't often see among presenters."Succession planningMany considered Winkleman, 54, to be chat show emperor Graham Norton's presumptive successor - not least because he seemed to be ushering her through himself.So Television, which Norton co-owns, also produced Winkleman's show, and it could have been a neat way for the company to retain work when Norton does eventually quit.Admittedly, Norton's show is not vanishing any time soon - he signed a new three-year deal with the BBC in 2025. He has also taken on several new projects, including a podcast, more novels, and a short-lived ITV game show, The Neighbourhood.But Norton, 63, has also spoken openly in recent years about working less. He reduced the number of chat show episodes he presents in 2022, and also stepped down from his Virgin Radio show two years later.Image source, BBC/So TelevisionImage caption, The BBC signed a new three-year deal with The Graham Norton Show in 2025The short life of The Claudia Winkleman Show could make the Norton succession plan a key issue for the BBC's incoming entertainment chief, Ed Havard. "This does leave the BBC with a problem if and when Graham decides to retire, because if Claudia can't do it, I don't know who can," says Singh."Graham doesn't want to do 52 weeks a year," Fincham notes, "so I'm sure the BBC would have been delighted to have another long-running chat show that you can balance with his, and they may have another try."Dozens of presenters would love the gig and many would be perfectly capable - Jack Whitehall did a solid job when he stood in for Norton previously, or Alan Carr could probably be tempted to return to his Chatty Man days. But the TV landscape is also littered with examples of cancelled chat shows. As well as Winkleman and McCall, Lily Allen and Charlotte Church also hosted series which didn't last long. Image caption, Winkleman will continue to host The Traitors and the forthcoming second series of its popular celebrity spin-offA cynic might say that the short life of Winkleman's series will have shown both her and the BBC that launching a new chat show is harder than it looks.But Kanter has a more nuanced interpretation, reflecting: "My instinct is that this was always a bit of an experiment. "Clearly it was something that Claudia wanted to do, and when you have a presenter at the peak of her powers, I think it's just good talent management to try and work together with that presenter on their dream project."He adds: "I'm sure all sides will walk away with their heads held high, and it was worth giving it a crack, I think."Do we still need chat shows?Personalities aside, there's the more existential question of whether the BBC even needs a new talk series, when there are now hundreds of other platforms where celebrities can go to promote their product. Stars can just as easily appear on YouTube strands such as Snack Wars or Hot Ones as a TV chat show, or spend as much time at press junkets being interviewed by TikTokers as legacy media outlets. Talent agents know that seeing Hollywood stars talking to a lovable and sweary East London pensioner, external known as Grime Gran, or playing a game of Would You Rather, external with LadBible, is just as likely to generate publicity as traditional interviews.Singh highlights that clips from programmes such as Norton's often go viral too, but adds: "I don't think the public is craving another TV chat show."Think back to the most memorable encounters from the heyday of chat shows," she says. "They were one-on-one: Parkinson with Muhammad Ali; Wogan with George Best or David Icke. "Those long-form interviews have moved to podcasts now, where celebrities find it easy to be open and essentially treat them as an extended therapy session. "And the most entertaining celebrity interviews around are on Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date. Compared to content like that, a chat show in a TV studio seems quite old-fashioned."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dimoldenberg interviews stars on Chicken Shop Date and now serves as the Oscars' red carpet reporterNorton's show clearly still delivers huge value for the BBC, and Kanter says the the "chat show format remains strong" and is a "really important part of the BBC One schedule"."It sprinkles a bit of stardust, it's appointment to view, I think people enjoy that it's a Friday night and they can tune in for some entertainment, it performs well online, it's an engine for clips and viral moments, and that's something that's to be valued in this attention economy," he notes.And, speaking from experience, Fincham concludes he is "not a big fan of succession plans" anyway."I ran BBC One between 2005 and 2007," he recalls, "and at that time, a regular conversation was 'What's the succession plan for David Attenborough?' "That was 20 years ago, and I can't help noticing he's still presenting programmes today. So beware of the assumption that a succession plan is needed. "And Graham Norton, if he chooses to continue, has got plenty more in the tank."

schema.headline: Who could be the next Graham Norton, and does the BBC even need one?

title: BuzzBallz are 'greenwashing' say recycling experts
description: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statem
body: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statement, which was deleted after the BBC contacted the company about this story, said it "loves our planet as much as we love a good cocktail" and partnered with TerraCycle to ensure its packaging gets recycled. However, TerraCycle, which involves consumers collecting packaging and sending it to be recycled, only runs the BuzzBallz scheme in the United States. BuzzBallz's UK FAQs, now also deleted, stated: "Yes, our packaging is recyclable. Please recycle your empties where local facilities allow."But no local facilities anywhere in the UK allow BuzzBallz to be recycled, said Adam Herriott, the head of packaging at WRAP."They're a mix of two very recyclable materials that put together makes an unrecyclable format."No local authorities will accept these at the kerbside."If they end up at a sorting facility, they could end up contaminating the plastic stream because of the metals in there and that could be very problematic for plastics recyclers that get into the machinery."But why should people care if their drink packaging is not recyclable?Even the shape of the BuzzBallz make it harder to be recycled because they can roll on the conveyor belts at the sorting facilities, said Herriott.  Among the machinery used, scanners can identify it in one position, but by the time air jets are used to separate it into the right recycling stream, it could have moved, meaning it could contaminate other streams. "It's definitely one of the villains of recycling," said Ambarish Mitra, co-founder of Greyparrot, a waste analytics company which helps recovery facilities. He said BuzzBallz have "have no recovery route in the current system" and "is a huge pet peeve for our customers and us".After analysing a plastic recover facility in Manchester with a processing capacity of 35,000 tonnes of plastic a year, for six months, the company found that BuzzBallz contaminated recycled plastic 66% of the time. "Once in the plastic stream, the aluminium reduces the quality of the recycled plastic, while the colour pigments can lower the recycled plastic bale's value."This isn't a recycling problem. It's a packaging problem."BuzzBallz refused to comment.James Piper, co-host of the Talking Rubbish podcast, co-owner of Ecosurety, said he dislikes BuzzBallz because of how difficult they are to recycle. "Every stage of the recycling journey has been designed around predictable packaging," Piper said. "When people come along and say, 'I'm going to make something different for marketing reasons', they are automatically making it more difficult for the recycler.""There's nothing environmentally positive about mixing packaging types."He said the BuzzBallz 'biggies' which have a plastic screw top lid is completely recyclable."Anyone can say on their website 'this is recyclable where your council allows'. But if no council allows it, then it doesn't mean anything," he said. BuzzBallz said: "We very recently went through a global website update and the information pertaining to TerraCycle recycling for BuzzBallz was incorrectly copied and does not apply to the UK market as of today. "We apologise for the oversight and have since updated our website to reflect the correct position for UK consumers."The company refused to comment on the now-deleted UK FAQs stating its packaging was recyclable.

title: Peterborough farm's delight after six white owlets found nesting
description: Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The owlets were ringed on Thursday by Simon DudhillByShariqua AhmedCambridgeA nest of six barn owlets has br
body: Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The owlets were ringed on Thursday by Simon DudhillByShariqua AhmedCambridgeA nest of six barn owlets has brought good news to a farm after a challenging period.The fluffy birds - which are estimated to be between 40 to 50 days old - were discovered at Moor Farm, near Peterborough, and were ringed on Thursday as part of ongoing conservation work.Judith Jacobs, the farm's owner, said the owlets were thriving and had lifted spirits after the farm was the target of six suspected arson attacks this summer.Simon Dudhill, who monitors the birds for Peterborough City Council's barn owl recovery scheme, said finding six owlets sharing a nest was "exceptionally good" and was the largest brood he had encountered in 2026.He added he had ringed more than 260 owlets in Cambridgeshire this year. Each bird from Moor Farm was fitted with a metal ring carrying a unique identification number issued by the British Trust for Ornithology. The ring's details allow conservationists to track individual birds and provides information about their movements. Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, Simon Dudhill said finding six owlets together was "exceptionally good"Jacobs said: "It's very exciting as we had none last year. We try and encourage wildlife as much as we can. "We have created a lot of hunting paths for the owls away from the main road, so they can hunt safely, because the biggest predators for barn owls are cars."She said the six owlets, which include three females and three males, are each about three days apart in age."Simon measured the length of their fourth feather, which tells their age, and from the colour of their feathers, if they are spotty they are females and the non-spotty ones are males," she added. Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The six owlets are each about three days apart in age and include three males and three femalesDudhill, who works for the Wildlife Conservation Partnership, external, said 2026 had been a much stronger breeding year for barn owls."I have ringed quite a few groups of five and four owlets this year. But this is the first  brood of six I have found," he added."Over the last couple of years, we have seen a decline in the number of babies but not adult barn owls. "Last year we found a lot of adults in boxes but they did not breed. This is all related to food. If there isn't enough food around, then they don't breed. "This year has been completely different. I personally found barn owl numbers have increased dramatically. But there are still some areas in Cambridgeshire that have not found as many babies as I have," he said. Despite monitoring barn owls for 15 years, Dudhill said the experience "never gets boring"."When you open a box, you have one or two or three little faces looking at you. It's just as exciting now as the first time I opened a box," he added. Do you have a story suggestion for Peterborough? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice
