title: The human cost of South Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveries
description: 'It eats away at my body': The human cost of S Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveriesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, South Korea's hug
body: 'It eats away at my body': The human cost of S Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveriesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, South Korea's huge delivery industry, powered by thousands of warehouse workers and riders, is under scrutinyByJake Kwon, Leehyun Choi and Hosu LeeReporting fromSeoulA week before her son died Park Mi-suk asked him to quit his job.For more than a year, the 27-year-old had been working overnight shifts at a warehouse for the country's largest online retailer, Coupang. He steered pallet movers with stacks of plastic bins and cardboard boxes across the sprawling space.In that time, Park says, her son lost 15kg and often complained of how tired he was.But Jang Deok-jun refused to quit. He compared his job to being on a seesaw: if he stepped down, his co-workers would struggle to keep going.The following week, Park found him unconscious and hunched over in the bath. "We pulled him out and performed first aid. We rushed him to hospital, where they declared him dead."Jang died of a heart attack. The state-run insurer that covers healthcare for workers, Comwel, blamed his death on overwork following an investigation.Park wishes she had noticed Jang's exhaustion sooner. "I didn't pay attention to my son's words, so I lost my son. But I hope others won't repeat the same mistake."Jang died in 2020 but six years on, Park is still fighting to end what she believes is the reason for his death: night-time deliveries.Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Jang Deok-jun was 27 years old when he died of a heart attackJang died as deliveries surged during the pandemic, which was often cited to explain his workload. But the working conditions for warehouse and delivery workers have been the subject of a growing national debate, with their union claiming that suspected deaths from overwork have continued.Night-time deliveries have become ubiquitous in hyper-connected South Korea, where shoppers are guaranteed delivery by 07:00 for orders placed before midnight. This convenience is thanks to a huge overnight workforce, from warehouse workers like Jang to delivery drivers.Several companies compete to offer speedy, cheap deliveries but the biggest is Coupang. Founded by a Korean-American, it became synonymous with online shopping in South Korea after 2015, when it started offering fresh produce overnight. It has grown to have an unrivalled network of warehouses and delivery trucks, with nearly 100,000 employees across the business.But increasingly, this industry is under scrutiny.Image source, BBC/Hosu LeeImage caption, Jang's mother Park Mi-suk says workers like her son are becoming invisibleBetween 2020 and May 2026, Comwel ruled that 46 warehouse and delivery workers, including Jang, died of a stroke or heart disease that count as work-related deaths. Jang aside, it's unclear how many of them worked overnight shifts.Comwel did not say how many of these cases were also investigated for the role of overwork, which only happens if the family asks for it in their claim. And not every case is referred to Comwel in the first place, so the data can be patchy.Previously Comwel data suggested that day-time delivery workers died of overwork and accidents at a higher rate than those who work overnight. But that is now questioned by those who say night-time deliveries are expanding fast, and there is not enough data to fully document their impact yet. The workers' union also argues that the latter is more harmful to health in the long-term.Night-time work is a probable cause of cancer globally, according to the UN's cancer research body, external. "Not only that, evidence has been accumulating that it also raises the risk of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and mental illness," says Kang Mo-yeol, professor of occupational medicine at the Catholic University of Korea.South Korea doesn't limit overnight working hours, unlike in the UK, where night-time delivery drivers cannot work more than 10 out of 24 hours. The Korean delivery workers' union called for a ban on overnight deliveries in 2025, but the union for Coupang's drivers says nearly all of their members prefer working at night. Some have children, elderly or ill family members to care for during the day and, more importantly, it pays better.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Coupang is the biggest of South Korea's online retailers "I can't do this for life because it eats away at my body," says Kim, a Coupang driver on a sub-contract, who did not want to share his real name. But he adds that his monthly salary of around 7m won ($4,600; £3,430) - nearly double the national average - makes it worth it.When the BBC met him at 22:00, he had already loaded his truck for the first round of deliveries.Driving through the narrow streets of Incheon city, west of the capital Seoul, he explains that he works from 21:00 to 07:00, five to six days a week.His schedule does not allow for a break. Every time the truck stops, he runs, package in hand. Nearly all drivers are paid by the number of packages they deliver and if they fail to make all deliveries by 07:00, they risk losing their "territory" to a competitor, he says.At first, his pregnant wife was scared he might fall asleep at the wheel. But he is used to it now, he insists, and he finds it easier to navigate the night's empty streets."We choose to deliver overnight for the money," Kim says. The way he sees it, those who are saying overnight deliveries should stop because they affect his health are ignoring the choice he has made. Image source, BBC/Hosu LeeImage caption, Kim said he is making good money as an overnight delivery driver, but his wife is worried he will fall asleep at the wheelBut men like Kim are becoming invisible, Jang's mother Park says, as the demand for fast deliveries grows, normalising the industry.Park spoke to the BBC outside Coupang's headquarters in Seoul's office district of Songpa. Standing alone in front of the gate, she told staff streaming out for lunch to remember her son and others like him. Few paid attention.Park says one of the challenges is how hard it is to hold employers accountable in cases like Jang's. She says it was on her to prove that her son had died from overwork, and Coupang was obligated to provide records, including security camera footage, to Comwel, but not her. After months of leaning on lawmakers and government agencies, she received Jang's work log and relevant CCTV footage.In the months before his death, Jang's working hours met the bar for how South Korean law defines deaths related to overwork: heart attacks or brain strokes after an average 60-hour-week over 12 weeks, or 64 hours a week in the four weeks leading up to death. Jang's overnight hours counted 30% more towards the calculation, according to Comwel's rules.Image source, BBC/Hosu LeeImage caption, Park outside Coupang's headquarters in Seoul, where she has been trying to draw attention to Jang's case As Park continued her fight, local media published what Coupang's former chief privacy officer claimed was a conversation with Chairman Bom Kim. In the leaked chat, Kim orders the executive to remove mentions of Jang "working hard" from internal reports: a phrase several employees used to describe Jang's final shift. Coupang called it a "groundless" claim by a disgruntled former executive.But the union accused the firm of covering up evidence and filed a criminal complaint. The police launched an investigation into Coupang in December 2025. Coupang denies the accusation, saying it had submitted everything that was requested and had fully cooperated with Comwel's investigation.By then, another high-profile case was in the headlines. Oh Seung-yong, 34, died after crashing his truck into a pole during a delivery run. It was an "occupational death", or work played a role, Comwel ruled.Oh's sister told parliament his work log showed that he had been working six days a week, more than 11 hours a day, and mostly at night. According to her, when their father had died days earlier, Oh delivered orders for another four hours before coming to hospital. He worked for a logistics company contracted by Coupang.Coupang says it restricts its employees to working for under 52 hours and gives sub-contracted drivers the full weekend off every two weeks. But the union alleges that this was not enforced by Oh's employer.The firm added that it fully pays for health check-ups for direct employees and sub-contracted drivers, and "has never had a single industrial accident death, which is the best safety record in the entire global logistics industry".Image source, SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Coupang boss Harold Rogers at South Korea's parliament Coupang CEO Harold Rogers was summoned to parliament in December 2025 over the deaths of Jang and Oh, as well as to answer for a recent data breach at his firm, involving 37.5 million users. The country's largest ever breach, it earned them a record $410m fine.During the televised hearing, Park demanded that Coupang's Chairman Kim be held accountable for her son's death, while Oh's sister asked for an apology from Rogers. He said he was "sorry" and offered his "deepest condolences". When Oh's sister pressed further, he was silent.The investigation into Coupang has also raised key questions for President Lee Jae Myung, who has a disability in his left arm from an old injury at a factory. He made it one of his priorities to reduce workplace injuries and deaths.Stories like Jang's and Oh's resonate deeply in South Korea, where gruelling work hours are no anomaly. It has one of the highest rates of workplace deaths among developed countries, a grim statistic it has been trying to improve for decades.The government has capped weekly work hours at 52 and passed a law to jail executives for negligence leading to workplace deaths. To break Coupang's stranglehold, the governing party even proposed relaxing existing restrictions so more retailers can deliver overnight. But the bill angered unions, activists and Park, who say the challenge goes beyond Coupang.Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Six years on from 27-year-old Jang's death, his mother still has his belongings"I've been haunting the streets since my son died," Park says.Because of all the time spent fighting for compensation and answers, she was forced to close her furniture-making business. She could no longer afford to live in her old home and moved to a rental apartment in Daegu city.She has kept all of Jang's belongings, including his collection of action figures. They sit in a box in her new apartment. She isn't ready to say goodbye yet, or to give up her fight.Recalling how Jang compared his work to riding a seesaw, where he held down one end, she says she sees it differently now. Jang and tens of thousands of workers like him are on one side for the convenience of the consumers on the other end, she says. "I hope we don't become a society where we close our eyes to others' sacrifice for a little convenience."

schema.headline: The human cost of South Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveries

title: Gangs, violence and dumped dead animals: The hidden world of illegal hare hunts
description: Image caption, Farmers say they have been threatened by balaclava-clad hare coursers at nightByDan AshbyLucy Taylor and Joseph LeeOn a remote Cambridg
body: Image caption, Farmers say they have been threatened by balaclava-clad hare coursers at nightByDan AshbyLucy Taylor and Joseph LeeOn a remote Cambridgeshire farm, where his nearest neighbour is half a mile away, Mathew Latta was making lunch when the peace was shattered by the sound of loud exhausts.Latta ran to the window to see a convoy of more than a dozen 4x4s heading towards his farm. His iron gates were cut open with an angle grinder and concrete blocks were shifted out of the way to clear the convoy's path.The vehicles drove right over his fields at speed, tearing up the crops and skirting the fence by the family's garden. Then more than 70 people got out of the vehicles, men dressed in military fatigues and balaclavas, cheering and playing music. Dogs were brought out on leads and began to hunt hares."They were all stood up on their cars with binoculars," says Latta. "I would say this is 100% a properly organised coursing event, with competitors and competitive dogs. People watching the course - and watching and betting on that sport. It was quite terrifying."Warning: This story contains images of dead animalsLatta and his family were trapped in their home. They kept calling the police, but nobody came. His daughter, then aged seven, was terrified and kept asking: "Are these men gonna come inside, daddy?"More than three hours later, the bloodsport was finally over and the crowd dispersed. They left behind four cars, one of them a burnt-out wreck. It emerged that, earlier that day, the convoy had rampaged through an area 20 miles (32km) long in the county, forcing other cars off the road and even robbing a petrol station.Image source, John Devine/BBC/Mathew LattaImage caption, Cars were abandoned on Mathew Latta's farm after it was taken over by hare coursersThis is the modern reality of hare coursing. It is an ancient sport where dogs such as greyhounds or lurchers are used to hunt hares, which the coursers usually scare out from the wild. Points are awarded for the number of times the dogs force the hare to twist and turn as it runs - as well as for the kill.The sport reached a peak of popularity in the 19th Century, but went underground after it was banned in the UK in 2005.We began investigating this underworld for the BBC Radio 4 podcast Dead Rabbit after the bodies of dead hares and other animals were mysteriously dumped in two picturesque Hampshire villages in 2024.In Awbridge, more than 20 carcasses - mostly hares and rabbits, along with a muntjac deer with a severed head - were strewn outside a primary school. Children were in tears when they arrived for lessons and found a horror-movie scene. About seven miles north, in Broughton, about 50 hares were scattered near the entrance of the village's community shop, with blood smeared on the doors and a dead barn owl and kestrel tied to the door handles.Image source, Crown Prosecution ServiceImage caption, Dozens of dead animals were strewn in front of the village shop in BroughtonWhat our investigation found was a hidden world of highly organised illegal bloodsport events taking place in rural areas, often by lamplight in the dead of night, with trophies, big money prizes, valuable hunting dogs and sometimes even international gambling. And it is all kept secret by organised crime gangs using intimidation and violence.'A proper operation'There have been almost 9,000 reports of hare coursing across the UK in the past three years, according to police responses to Freedom of Information Act requests by the BBC.The figures are not definitive - some incidents may have been reported more than once, while others may not have been reported at all - but in the absence of official crime figures for illegal hare coursing, they give us an indication of the scale of the problem.Cambridgeshire Constabulary says it was "very stretched" on the January day last year when Mathew Latta's farm was invaded, and the force says it did not respond the way it would have wanted. Supt Ben Martin tells us that the coursers had rampaged through the county deliberately, to distract police and send them to the wrong places.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Until the 2005 ban, hare coursing used to take place at well-attended events such as the Waterloo CupHaving been caught out, the force stepped up its efforts to investigate who was behind the illegal event, eventually arresting more than 40 people and charging 25, several of whom have now been convicted.As officers tracked down the coursers, it turned out they had come from all over the country: Lincolnshire, Leicestershire, Berkshire, north Wales. "People had come hundreds of miles to be there that day," says Martin. "It was a proper operation."Then, after searching an address belonging to one of the arrested men, police found the trophy the coursers had been competing for - the Super 8 Cup, etched with images of dogs and hares, standing maybe 2ft (61cm) tall, about the size of the FA Cup.The invasion of Latta's farm had been a highlight of the illegal hare coursing calendar, a recurring cup competition whose previous winners are engraved on the base of the trophy - both the owners and the dogs, which had names such as "Beyoncé" and "Bunny".Buried - Dead RabbitA husband and wife team up with Chris Packham to investigate why 20 dead animals were left at a village school - uncovering a criminal underworld in the British countryside.'Like a small army'A scene after the cup final last year, captured on video obtained by the BBC, shows how hare coursing involves serious money. A group of eight men can be seen drinking pints in a pub and shouting, as they haggle over a lurcher standing on the table before them. The dog was the Super 8 Cup champion of 2025 and sold for £55,000.It is not the only evidence of the cash that flows through the illegal bloodsport: we were told the Super 8 Cup prize was about £50,000, while the entry fee for the competition was £1,000, as revealed by a seized phone belonging to one of the kingpins. Police say this cash funds the prize money and covers expenses, such as a pool of vehicles and even court costs in case the hare coursers are raided.Ch Insp Kevin Lacks-Kelly, head of the UK National Wildlife Crime Unit, tells the BBC that money had also flowed into the illegal sport through livestreams for gamblers in China on one or two occasions. But he says the gangs in the UK did not need overseas bets to fund their illicit hobby.Image caption, The Super 8 Cup is now kept in a police storage roomHare coursers were linked to crimes involving significant sums of money, says Lacks-Kelly, not "minimum-wage crimes". "Some of these lads are making a fortune. You've got some of the country's best organised criminals," he adds.There are some localised events that still just involve a handful of men and dogs, Lacks-Kelly says, but the level of organisation in bigger events "has increased tenfold" with the influx of organised crime."They've got the advantage in numbers. And they will go anywhere and do anything and commit this crime at all costs," he says."They're like a small army, just do what they want, don't they? Turn up en masse, block roads off, drive over fields, cause damage, dump the cars, burn the cars out. Mass participation events that are designed to overwhelm."Image caption, Farmers say their vehicles have sometimes been rammed by hare coursersLacks-Kelly says his team has homed in on 27 of the country's worst offenders for hare coursing and all but five of them have links to organised crime."These are violent criminals that abuse people, animals, women. Carry weapons, firearms, and make threats. These are not the people that you want in your community," he says.'No-one's gonna hear you scream'The BBC contacted members of the Country Land and Business Association, which represents 30,000 rural landowners and businesses in England and Wales, to ask about their experiences with hare coursing.About 50 responded, nearly all of them saying their land or property had been damaged. Someone in Cheshire said it happened every week, a farmer in Essex said it had happened more than 100 times, while one in North Yorkshire said 150 times.And 29 of the respondents said they had been threatened with violence.According to the survey responses, hare coursers had threatened to kidnap farmers' dogs, shouted that they would burn their buildings down, had thrown bricks through windows, made anonymous phone threats to stab them in the neck, used catapults to fire ball-bearings at them, rammed and damaged vehicles with people inside, and warned the farmers that they knew where they lived and where their kids go to school.Wiltshire farmer David Lemon showed us his 3,000-acre farm, where hare coursers have previously torn up the fields with miles of tyre tracks. He has tried to fortify the land, closing off gateways, putting in concrete blocks or piles of logs, and digging rows of deep ditches to make it undrivable. But they still get in and, when he has tried to confront them, he has been threatened.Image caption, David Lemon says he has been threatened by balaclava-clad figures when he has interrupted hare coursingIn his vast, isolated farm, a confrontation at night means "no-one's gonna hear you scream", he says."First thing you see is a face with a balaclava on, with a catapult in his hand with ball bearings in," he says. "That's one eye gone. And is it worth the struggle?"He fears that someone will get killed before long - either because a farmer overreacts to the intrusion or the hare coursers take their intimidation tactics too far."You get red mist when you see them trashing your years' work and this is all you've got. And they're just trashing it," says Lemon. "This is not fair. You can't be hostage in your own home. This is our farm. This is our home."Elsewhere in the county, a woman who called police on hare coursers at her father's farm received rape threats on social media as a result, according to Wiltshire Police and Crime Commissioner Phillip Wilkinson.'We can do what we want'One gamekeeper was run over and badly injured when he tried to confront hare coursers on land he managed, says Tim Weston from the National Gamekeepers' Organisation."He broke both his legs, pelvis, ruptured lungs." Weston says. "They left at high speed, potentially could have left him for dead." Fortunately, the man is now back and work and recovering, he said.As we talked, it turned out that Weston, who is now based in Wiltshire, grew up in a village near Broughton in Hampshire, where the animals were dumped outside the shop. In 2024, he was working in deer management on an estate where he suspects the dead hares had been killed.The night before they were dumped, there had been wheel marks across the estate, he says. The local gamekeeper had stopped the hare coursers three or four times.Weston says the abandoned animals were a message to say: "We've been. You didn't catch us this time."Using dead animals to taunt landowners is common, Weston says. In our survey of farmers and landowners, 35 of the respondents said animal bodies had been deliberately left on their land.It is a message to the local community that "we can do what we want because no-one's going to police it", Weston says.Image source, Crown Prosecution ServiceImage caption, CCTV showed two men dumping the dead animals in BroughtonHampshire Police did arrest a man over the dumped animals at Broughton community shop, however. The force commissioned a forensic analysis of the dead kestrel and barn owl left on the doors and took DNA samples. James Kempster, a man who police say had a prior record of wildlife crimes, was arrested as a result.At trial, Kempster denied he had abandoned the animals. CCTV footage of two men casually tossing dozens of dead hares outside the shop - one of them ripping one of the bodies in half to smear its blood around - were not clear enough to reveal their identities.Kempster was convicted of handling the dead birds, a crime in itself because they are protected species. But he was found not guilty of criminal damage - the charge that related to abandoning the carcasses.So was the incident really a warning or a taunt to the local community from hare coursers? With the perpetrators still unidentified, their motive cannot be known for certain.One police officer recalls an arrangement of dead animals' whose message seemed undeniable, however. He tells us how he had sometimes found bodies strung over speed limit signs and street furniture in villages or left outside people's houses.Once, he says, he had seen them laid out in the road, the corpses spelling out the words: "Catch me".

schema.headline: Gangs, violence and dumped dead animals: The hidden world of illegal hare hunts
